title: NNL Commends BetPawa, TSM, Others For Backing Successful Season - LEADERSHIP Newspapers
content: The board of the Nigeria National League (NNL) has praised its sponsors — BetPawa, Toptier Sports Management (TSM), Prostar International and Sportslight Hub — for their contributions towards the successful staging of the 2025/2026 league season. The commendation was contained in a communiqué issued after the league body’s end-of-season board meeting held on Tuesday, 5 May 2026, at the auditorium of Beyond Limits FC in Ikenne, Ogun State. In the communiqué, the NNL board highlighted the positive impact of the sponsors’ support on the growth and smooth organisation of the country’s second-tier football league. “We want to use this opportunity to commend BetPawa for the prompt implementation of the Locker Room Bonuses during the 2025/2026 league season, as well as the introduction of end-of-season awards for outstanding performers,” the communiqué stated. The board also applauded Toptier Sports Management (TSM) for its investment in the league, noting that the company’s involvement has helped to raise standards within the NNL. “It is equally important that we thank Toptier Sports Management (TSM) for its laudable investment in the Nigeria National League. Their support has further raised the bar in the NNL,” the statement added. content: After several consecutive years of surging as NVIDIA's top-performing “shadow stock” in Asian markets, $Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM.US)$ it is now increasingly competing with other artificial intelligence (AI) concept stocks for investor attention. As mainstream adoption of AI drives demand for hardware beyond NVIDIA’s high-end chips, equity traders are chasing a broader set of beneficiaries. Multiple AI sub-themes—from tightening supply of memory chips to advances in robotics—are also drawing capital inflows. Meanwhile, single-stock position limits are prompting funds to diversify their holdings. Retail investors, who have long been familiar with Taiwan Semiconductor through American Depositary Receipts (ADRs), now also have more alternative Asian tech stocks to choose from. As a result, Taiwan Semiconductor’s stock has underperformed MediaTek—a chip design company—by the widest margin since 2009 this year. At the same time, the market capitalization gap between Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung Electronics, the world’s largest memory chipmaker, has significantly narrowed, with the latter also joining the 'trillion-dollar market cap club.' Jason Hsu, Chief Investment Officer at Rayliant Global Advisors in Boston, stated that the market is witnessing a 'structural shift away from Taiwan Semiconductor toward other companies.' He added that newly raised fund capital 'is flowing disproportionately into other tech firms that are also benefiting from record AI-related capital expenditures.' Although Taiwan Semiconductor’s share price has risen 44% this year—supported by strong sales and earnings—it has lagged behind MediaTek and Samsung Electronics, whose shares have each gained nearly 150%. This mirrors NVIDIA’s situation: despite continued robust growth, its stock performance has started to trail some other AI-related equities. There is little doubt that Taiwan Semiconductor, as the manufacturer of virtually all of NVIDIA’s advanced GPUs (graphics processing units), will continue benefiting from AI demand for the foreseeable future. However, as AI increasingly shifts toward the 'inferencing' phase—focused on executing specific tasks—other players are emerging as new winners. Hot trades are emerging among chip design companies—for example, MediaTek is assisting Google in developing application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs). Meanwhile, demand is also rising for central processing units (CPUs), which are relatively less technologically demanding and can be manufactured not only by Taiwan Semiconductor but also by foundries operated by Samsung and Intel (INTC.US). Brian Ooi, Portfolio Manager at Swiss-Asia Financial Services Pte., said, 'Agent-based AI is broadening the scope of AI-related trades because AI agents require more CPUs.' He added, 'As AI spending shifts from the training phase to the inferencing phase, I expect this diffusion trend to persist and become the next leg of the AI trade.' Moreover, because Taiwan Semiconductor focuses on logic chips, it does not directly benefit from the current boom in memory and data storage devices—a trend that has driven significant share price gains for Samsung and its peers. Global investors will soon gain easier access to these memory-related equities, as South Korea’s SK Hynix and Japan’s Kioxia Holdings both plan to launch ADRs this year. Asian firms also feature prominently in the newly launched and popular Roundhill Memory ETF, and U.S. retail investors can now even trade Korean stocks directly online. Another reason for Taiwan Semiconductor’s relative underperformance is that many actively managed funds impose a 10% cap on single-stock holdings. Given that Taiwan Semiconductor now accounts for over 40% of the weight in the Taiwan Weighted Index, these funds are compelled to buy other stocks to keep pace with the benchmark index. Jian Shi Cortesi, a portfolio manager at GAM Investment Management in Zurich, said: 'I already hold a position in Taiwan Semiconductor close to 10%, and over the past few months, I have further increased allocations to **** tech stocks driven by AI demand.' She added that these companies include those engaged in chip packaging, power management, thermal solutions, and printed circuit boards (PCBs). Kevin Net, Head of Asian Equities at Financiere de l’Echiquier, noted that due to the 10% holding limit, his fund is 'structurally underweight Taiwan Semiconductor,' but has raised its 'non-Taiwan Semiconductor AI exposure' by 5% compared to earlier this year. He stated that his investment targets include MediaTek, Samsung Electronics, as well as Taiwan’s ASE Group and Chroma ATE, as these companies are also poised to benefit from Taiwan Semiconductor’s capital expenditures.
